question: How many links make up the standard chain of infection?
explanation: You've got this! The chain of infection is made up of six links, starting from the infectious agent all the way to the susceptible host. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h1)

question: What happens when you wash your hands and stop a germ from reaching a patient?

options.C: A link in the chain of infection is broken
options.D: The patient becomes immune to all diseases

explanation: Spot on! Simple actions like hand hygiene interrupt transmission, effectively breaking the chain and keeping your patient safe. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h1)

question: What do we call someone who carries and spreads a germ without looking or feeling sick?
explanation: Correct! Asymptomatic carriers harbor and spread germs while feeling completely healthy themselves. That's why universal precautions matter so much! [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which of these is a non-living place where germs can hang out and multiply?

options.C: A nurse with a skin infection

explanation: Well done! Things like water, soil, and medical equipment are non-living (inanimate) sources that can store and grow pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h2)

question: In nursing, what is a 'fomite'?

options.A: An inanimate object that harbors germs
options.B: A chemical used to clean wounds

explanation: You nailed it! Fomites are non-living items like BP cuffs, tables, or stethoscopes that can pass germs from one person to another. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h3)

question: A patient gets a wound infection after a nurse uses an uncleaned blood pressure cuff. What kind of spread is this?
explanation: Great job! The uncleaned cuff acts as a fomite, carrying the germ indirectly from one patient to the next. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h3)

question: How does a respiratory virus normally leave the body?
explanation: Exactly! Respiratory germs love to catch a ride on droplets expelled through the nose and mouth when someone coughs or sneezes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h4)

question: Why does putting in a urinary catheter raise a patient's risk of getting an infection?

options.A: It stops the kidneys from producing urine
options.B: It turns the skin into a non-living reservoir
options.C: It destroys all white blood cells in the bladder
options.D: It creates an artificial pathway for bacteria to enter

explanation: Spot on! Catheters bypass the body's natural defenses, giving bacteria a direct highway into the urinary tract. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h4)

question: What does 'susceptible host' mean in the chain of infection?

options.A: A person who transmits viruses through the air
options.B: A person who is completely immune to all germs
options.C: A person whose body cannot easily fight off an invading germ
options.D: A person who acts as a permanent reservoir for bacteria

explanation: You got it! A susceptible host simply lacks the immunity or strength to stop a pathogen from causing an infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which group of patients is usually most at risk for catching hospital-acquired infections?
explanation: Correct! Older age plus medications that lower immunity make these patients much more vulnerable to infections. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h5)

question: During which stage of an infection do mild, general symptoms like tiredness first show up before full sickness hits?
explanation: Well done! The prodromal stage is that early phase where a patient just feels 'off' or unusually tired before specific symptoms appear. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why is a patient in the prodromal stage often a high risk for spreading germs to others?

options.A: Their immune system has completely stopped functioning
options.B: They feel well enough to move around while carrying germs
options.C: They shed the highest volume of toxic waste products
options.D: Pathogens multiply exclusively during this specific phase

explanation: Spot on! Because they don't feel super sick yet, they keep moving around and unknowingly expose people around them. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the single most important nursing action to stop the spread of hospital infections?

options.B: Changing bed linens once an hour

explanation: You nailed it! Good hand hygiene is your superpower as a nurse—it washes away germs and stops them in their tracks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h7)

question: You wear sterile gloves and a mask while putting in a urinary catheter. Which link in the infection chain are you mainly trying to block?
explanation: Awesome! Using sterile barriers blocks germs from sneaking into vulnerable places like the urinary tract. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h7)
